items.stem: A nonsterile automated compounder handles a penicillin formulation, then an unrelated drug. Residue cannot be removed from an internal channel by any validated cleaning method. What must the pharmacy establish before sequential use?

choices.text: Continue production when the same trained technician operates both batches.
choices.why: Incorrect. The memo requires confirmation that the device is readily cleanable; a consistent operator does not replace residue controls.

choices.text: Use the manufacturer's marketing statement of accuracy to establish drug-residue clearance.
choices.why: Incorrect. Accuracy claims do not demonstrate cleanability or absence of cross-contamination.

choices.text: Resolve whether the machine is cleanable enough to minimize drug cross-contamination.
choices.why: Correct. The Board explicitly requires pharmacies to confirm device cleanability to minimize cross-contamination.

choices.text: Assign a shorter beyond-use date to the second product and skip the cleaning question.
choices.why: Incorrect. A changed BUD does not remedy possible cross-contamination introduced by uncleanable equipment.

items.citation: Board Memorandum 2025-11-06: Automated Non-Sterile Compounding Devices ¶3; 247 CMR 9.01(3)
items.novelty_rationale: New operational cleanability question versus D029 device validation and D030 API compatibility.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational questions; not real secure MPJE items.

items.stem: A 503A pharmacy has manufacturer validation for its automated nonsterile compounder. Its manager wants to delete master-formulation and batch-specific records because the machine prints a summary. Which responsibility remains?

choices.text: The pharmacy remains accountable for product quality and applicable compounding records.
choices.why: Correct. The Board memorandum expressly retains pharmacy responsibility regardless of equipment; 247 CMR 9.01(3) retains applicable USP compounding standards.

choices.text: The manufacturer assumes all final compounded-product accountability when it validates the machine.
choices.why: Incorrect. Validation does not transfer pharmacy responsibility to the maker.

choices.text: Device validation exempts the 503A pharmacy from all USP <795> preparation documentation.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Board requires continued compliance with USP chapters despite automation.

choices.text: The pharmacy becomes an FDA-registered 503B outsourcing facility by purchasing the device.
choices.why: Incorrect. Federal 503B status is a separate registration model, not conferred by a device purchase.

items.citation: Board Memorandum 2025-11-06 introductory paragraph and ¶¶1–3; 247 CMR 9.01(3)
items.novelty_rationale: Who retains quality/recordkeeping responsibility in automation, not E30-095 503A vs 503B office-stock eligibility.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational questions; not real secure MPJE items.

items.stem: Rx A, a signed Schedule II prescription, names Patient A. The prescriber asks to replace the name with Patient B. Rx B is validly signed for the correct patient but lacks the prescriber's DEA number; the pharmacist independently verifies it. Which actions comply with Board Policy 2018-01? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Request a new Rx in Patient B's name rather than altering the named patient on Rx A.
choices.why: Correct. The policy lists changing to a different patient as information that cannot be changed on any schedule; new prescription is required.

choices.text: Replace Patient A with Patient B by documenting that the prescriber authorized the patient switch.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient name to a different patient is expressly non-correctable even when the office contacts the pharmacist.

choices.text: For Rx B, add the verified prescriber's DEA number without prescriber consultation, documenting the addition.
choices.why: Correct. The Schedule II policy allows the prescriber DEA number to be added without consultation; all changes must be documented.

choices.text: Hold Rx B until the prescriber signs a replacement paper form because adding a DEA number is forbidden.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Board's listed permission for adding an omitted DEA number avoids a blanket requirement for a new prescription.

items.novelty_rationale: Two-row document: irreversible patient change vs verification-based missing DEA number, with distinct legal outcomes.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational questions; not real secure MPJE items.

items.stem: An intermediary drops the quantity from a correctly signed Schedule II EPCS order during transmission. Other fields arrive intact. The intermediary cites the federal permission to convert software field formats. What is the federal effect?

choices.text: The prescription remains valid because all electronic field conversions are exempt from audit.
choices.why: Incorrect. Changing data structure is permissible; losing required Part 1306 content is not.

choices.text: Reconstruct the quantity from the patient's last fill and proceed without prescriber authorization.
choices.why: Incorrect. A prior record does not repair an invalid prescription whose required data were altered in transmission.

choices.text: The prescription may be filled if the patient verbally verifies the missing quantity.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient recollection is not prescriber authentication for missing required controlled prescription content.

choices.text: Loss of a required prescription field invalidates the transmitted EPCS order.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1311.170(e) treats changed, truncated or removed required content during electronic transmission as invalid, while permitting lossless format conversions.

items.novelty_rationale: Different EPCS data-integrity event from a harmless change in machine-readable field structure.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational questions; not real secure MPJE items.

items.stem: A validly signed Schedule II Rx comes from a DEA-registered physician. The pharmacist finds a serious unresolved inconsistency in therapeutic purpose and competing controlled prescriptions. The office confirms only the DEA number, not medical legitimacy. What action is appropriate?

choices.text: Dispense because the prescriber signature and DEA registration are valid.
choices.why: Incorrect. 21 CFR 1306.04(a) requires legitimate medical purpose and places a corresponding duty on the pharmacist; a valid number does not resolve an unexplained substantive red flag.

choices.text: Hold dispensing and investigate unresolved medical-purpose concerns using appropriate evidence.
choices.why: Correct. Authenticity and registration are not substitutes for a good-faith legitimacy inquiry when material red flags remain.

choices.text: Ask the technician to determine whether the patient's diagnosis justifies all controlled prescriptions.
choices.why: Incorrect. Technician data collection does not replace the pharmacist's professional legal and clinical responsibility.

choices.text: Call the insurer for payment confirmation and regard approval as a medical-purpose finding.
choices.why: Incorrect. Financial adjudication does not establish legitimate medical purpose under the DEA rule.

items.novelty_rationale: Separates authentic prescriber identity from unresolved medical legitimacy; tests evidence rather than mere red-flag word recognition.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational questions; not real secure MPJE items.

items.stem: An authorized prescriber-office agent calls about a Schedule II prescription, confirming a corrected patient street address. The agent also asks the pharmacist to replace the prescriber's name and signature with another physician from the same clinic. Which actions are permitted? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Correct the patient's street address after consultation with the prescriber or authorized agent, with required documentation.
choices.why: Correct. Board/DCP Policy 2018-01 permits a changed patient address with consultation, including an authorized agent.

choices.text: Rewrite the prescriber's identity and signature because both physicians share the clinic.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy bars changing a prescriber's name or signature on prescriptions in any Schedule II–VI.

choices.text: Request a new prescription if the intent is to substitute the other prescriber as the issuing practitioner.
choices.why: Correct. The originating prescriber identity/signature is non-correctable and requires a new prescription to change.

choices.text: Treat the office employee's statement as a substitute for a new prescription signed by the different physician.
choices.why: Incorrect. An employee callback cannot replace issuing a lawful new prescription when a prohibited field is changed.

items.novelty_rationale: Differentiatable verified-agent patient-address correction vs prescriber identity replacement, not routine Rx missing fields.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational questions; not real secure MPJE items.

items.stem: A federal drug-schedule reference from November 2026 lists tramadol and O-desmethyltramadol (desmetramadol, O-DSMT). Although one is a metabolite of the other, what is the correct current federal classification?

choices.text: Tramadol Schedule III; O-desmethyltramadol Schedule III.
choices.why: Incorrect. Tramadol is Schedule IV; the metabolite has a separate temporary Schedule I listing.

choices.text: Both are Schedule IV because DEA schedules active metabolites with parent medicines.
choices.why: Incorrect. A distinct scheduling action placed O-DSMT in Schedule I effective August 12, 2026.

choices.text: Tramadol Schedule IV; O-desmethyltramadol temporarily Schedule I.
choices.why: Correct. Tramadol is controlled under 21 CFR 1308.14(b)(3); O-DSMT was temporarily placed in Schedule I in 2026.

choices.text: Neither is scheduled because the metabolite occurs during legitimate therapy.
choices.why: Incorrect. Metabolism does not exempt a separately listed manufactured/handled substance from the CSA.

items.novelty_rationale: New 2026 temporary federal scheduling action, distinct from existing standard tramadol questions.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational questions; not real secure MPJE items.

items.stem: An otherwise valid Massachusetts prescription is for AUVELITY (dextromethorphan/bupropion) extended-release tablets. FDA labels the ingredients federally noncontrolled. What is its Massachusetts Schedule and MassPAT status?

choices.text: Schedule V, with regular Massachusetts PMP submission.
choices.why: Incorrect. Dextromethorphan/bupropion is not federally controlled as specified in the FDA label.

choices.text: Schedule VI; not subject to routine MassPAT reporting absent an added reportable ingredient.
choices.why: Correct. Massachusetts Schedule VI covers prescription drugs outside I–V; DPH requires reporting for II–V and gabapentin, not each VI prescription.

choices.text: Federal noncontrolled and Massachusetts Schedule VI; every VI drug must be reported to MassPAT.
choices.why: Incorrect. MA reporting requirements do not extend to all Schedule VI drugs; gabapentin is the specifically identified drug of concern.

choices.text: Federal Schedule II and Massachusetts Schedule II because it is indicated for neuropsychiatric treatment.
choices.why: Incorrect. Clinical indication does not determine CSA Schedule; the FDA label states no controlled substances.

items.citation: FDA AUVELITY label (2026) §9.1; 105 CMR 700.002(F); 105 CMR 700.012; DPH PMP pharmacy reporting
items.novelty_rationale: New real combination drug and Massachusetts reporting contrast with gabapentin (E30-039 and C078).
items.copyright_policy: Original educational questions; not real secure MPJE items.

items.stem: FDA-labeled LIBRAX (chlordiazepoxide/clidinium) is verified on DEA's exempted prescription list. Compare it with single-ingredient chlordiazepoxide. Which federal and Massachusetts classification is correct?

choices.text: Both products must be Schedule IV because they contain chlordiazepoxide.
choices.why: Incorrect. A specifically exempted finished combination is treated differently from the separately controlled benzodiazepine ingredient.

choices.text: Neither product can be scheduled because antispasmodic drugs are outside CSA regulations.
choices.why: Incorrect. Chlordiazepoxide itself remains federal Schedule IV.

choices.text: LIBRAX becomes Schedule II because it contains an anticholinergic ingredient.
choices.why: Incorrect. Combining drugs does not make the product Schedule II absent an applicable classification.

choices.text: Chlordiazepoxide alone is IV; listed LIBRAX is federally exempt and MA Schedule VI.
choices.why: Correct. DEA's active product-specific exemption removes qualifying Librax from federal Schedule IV; MA Schedule VI applies to prescription drugs not scheduled I–V.

items.citation: 21 CFR 1308.14(c)(10); 21 CFR 1308.31–.32; DEA Exempted Prescription Product Table (chlordiazepoxide/clidinium); FDA Librax Drug Abuse and Dependence label; 105 CMR 700.002(F)
items.novelty_rationale: Non-butyrlbital exact product-specific listed exemption; avoids E30-189's Fioricet/other butalbital NDC scenario.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational questions; not real secure MPJE items.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy has two valid outpatient orders for opioid-use-disorder treatment. Order X is VIVITROL (naltrexone extended-release IM). Order Y is BRIXADI (buprenorphine extended-release injection). The products' FDA labels and applicable REMS are current. Which classifications and handling distinctions are accurate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: VIVITROL is not federally controlled and falls under Massachusetts Schedule VI as an ordinary prescription drug.
choices.why: Correct. FDA's Vivitrol label states it is not a controlled substance; Massachusetts places other prescription drugs into Schedule VI.

choices.text: BRIXADI is a federal Schedule III buprenorphine product and its REMS restricts dispensing directly to a healthcare provider for administration.
choices.why: Correct. The FDA Brixadi label identifies the Schedule III substance and direct-to-provider REMS distribution controls.

choices.text: Both are federal Schedule II simply because they are used to treat opioid-use disorder.
choices.why: Incorrect. An indication for OUD does not set the drug's schedule; naltrexone is not controlled and buprenorphine is III.

choices.text: The pharmacist may dispense BRIXADI directly to the patient for unsupervised self-injection when the prescription is valid.
choices.why: Incorrect. The FDA BRIXADI REMS forbids direct patient dispensing and requires provider administration.

items.citation: FDA VIVITROL controlled substance status; FDA BRIXADI 2026 label §§5.2–5.3; 21 CFR 1308.13(e)(2); MA 105 CMR 700.002
items.novelty_rationale: Two real long-acting OUD injections with opposite federal schedule status and distinctive REMS custody; not basic Suboxone identification.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational questions; not real secure MPJE items.
